questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the systolic blood pressure target for a pediatric patient in anaphylactic shock?
questions.explanation: Pediatric anaphylactic shock is targeted to an age-adjusted SBP > 90 + (age x 2); the flat SBP > 90 target is the adult value.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: After analgesia and beta blockade, an aortic dissection patient still has an elevated heart rate. Which second-line agent does the chart direct?
questions.explanation: For aortic emergencies the second-line agent for a persistently elevated HR is diltiazem; nicardipine or NTG are reserved for persistently elevated BP.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: After analgesia and beta blockade, an aortic dissection patient remains hypertensive with a controlled heart rate. Which second-line agent does the chart direct?
questions.explanation: Second line for elevated BP in an aortic emergency is nicardipine or NTG, added only after aggressive analgesia and beta blockade; diltiazem is for an elevated HR.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: An aortic emergency patient stays hypotensive after all vasoactive, analgesic and sedative drips are turned off. Norepinephrine is started to what systolic goal?
questions.explanation: If hypotension persists, norepinephrine is titrated to a palpable radial pulse, SBP > 60 or improved mentation — a deliberately permissive goal to limit shear stress on the aorta.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: Above what systolic pressure is antihypertensive treatment started for an atraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Atraumatic ICH is targeted to SBP 140 - 150, so treatment begins once SBP exceeds 150; 180 and 220 are ischemic stroke limits.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the second-line antihypertensive for an atraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage above target?
questions.explanation: After elevating the head of bed and treating pain, ICH above SBP 150 is treated with nicardipine or labetalol — titratable agents that avoid overshoot.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: While a norepinephrine infusion is being set up for cardiogenic shock, what may be used to support blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock (SBP > 90 target) is treated with fluids then norepinephrine; push dose epinephrine may bridge until the infusion is running.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the minimum systolic blood pressure target for a 6-year-old in hemorrhagic shock with head trauma?
questions.explanation: Children under 10 in hemorrhagic shock with head trauma are targeted to 90 + (age x 2) = 102, higher than the SBP > 80 used without head trauma to protect cerebral perfusion.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the systolic target for a child in hemorrhagic shock without head trauma?
questions.explanation: Without head trauma, pediatric hemorrhagic shock is targeted to SBP > 80 (permissive); the age-adjusted 90 + (age x 2) applies only when there is head trauma.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: Fluids, blood and procedural treatments have not restored the target in hemorrhagic shock. What is the first second-line agent?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic shock second line is push dose epinephrine first, then a norepinephrine or epinephrine infusion — and only after fluid/blood resuscitation is under way.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the systolic target for an adult with non-traumatic hypovolemia?
questions.explanation: Non-trauma hypovolemia in adults is targeted to SBP 80 – 90 with fluids; epinephrine or norepinephrine are added only if BP is refractory.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: Below what mean arterial pressure should an ischemic stroke patient not be allowed to fall?
questions.explanation: Both thrombolytic and non-thrombolytic ischemic stroke rows require maintaining SBP > 100/70 (MAP > 80) to preserve penumbral perfusion while treating the upper limit.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: Which vasopressor is second line for a hypotensive patient with a spinal injury after fluids?
questions.explanation: Spinal injuries & shock target SBP > 90; fluids are first line and norepinephrine is the second-line vasopressor.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: First-line labetalol or hydralazine has not controlled blood pressure in pre-eclampsia. What is second line?
questions.explanation: Second line for pre-eclampsia, eclampsia and PIH is a labetalol/hydralazine infusion, treating until both SBP 140 – 150 and DBP 90 - 100 are met.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: What is the blood pressure target after return of spontaneous circulation?
questions.explanation: Post-ROSC care targets SBP > 90 mmHg or MAP > 65, with fluids first, then epinephrine and norepinephrine.

questions.title: Blood Pressure Treatment Chart
questions.stem: Fluids have not met the blood pressure target after ROSC. Which vasopressor is listed first?
questions.explanation: After ROSC the chart lists epinephrine then norepinephrine — the reverse of adult sepsis, where norepinephrine is first.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: What is the normal cardiac index?
questions.explanation: Cardiac index is cardiac output adjusted for body size, so its normal 2.5 - 4 is lower than the 4 - 8 L/min cardiac output range (the table prints L/min; it is normally indexed per m2).

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: What is the normal mean pulmonary artery pressure?
questions.explanation: Mean PA pressure, the average pressure in the arteries leading from the heart to the lungs, is normally 9 - 16 mmHg; 5 - 12 is PCWP.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: What is the normal right atrial pressure?
questions.explanation: Right atrial pressure is normally 2 - 6 mmHg; the table lists central venous pressure separately as 0 - 8 mmHg.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: What does pulmonary vascular resistance reflect?
questions.explanation: PVR (normal 155 - 255 dyn/sec/cm-5) is the resistance to RV ejection offered by pulmonary pressure, i.e. RV afterload; SVR is its LV counterpart.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: What does central venous pressure reflect?
options: RV filling pressure and mean systemic venous pressure
LV filling pressure across the pulmonary capillaries
Resistance to RV ejection by pulmonary pressure
Resistance to LV ejection by aortic pressure
questions.explanation: CVP (0 - 8 mmHg) reflects right-sided filling — RV filling pressure and mean systemic venous pressure — not left-sided filling, which PCWP estimates.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is used to estimate which pressure?
questions.explanation: PCWP reflects LV filling pressure, valid only if no obstruction exists between the catheter balloon tip and the LV.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: When is pulmonary capillary wedge pressure a valid reflection of left ventricular filling pressure?
options: When the patient is off positive pressure ventilation
When cardiac output is within 4 - 8 L/min
When there is no obstruction between the catheter balloon tip and the LV
When right atrial pressure is within 2 - 6 mmHg
questions.explanation: The table qualifies PCWP: it reflects LV filling pressure only if nothing obstructs the path from balloon tip to LV.

questions.title: Hemodynamic Pressure Table
questions.stem: How does the table define stroke volume?
options: Blood ejected into the systemic circulation per minute
Cardiac output adjusted for body size
Average arterial pressure during one cardiac cycle
Blood ejected from the left ventricle with each heartbeat
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is the per-beat LV ejection; multiplied by heart rate it gives cardiac output (blood ejected per minute), and indexed to body size gives cardiac index.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: During the EMS VAN vision test, what finding is considered positive?
options: Failure to count fingers correctly or double vision
Inability to follow an object with both eyes
Inability to identify which arm is touched
questions.explanation: VAN vision is tested by counting fingers in all 4 quadrants and tracking a finger for diplopia; failure to count fingers or double vision is positive. Forced gaze and arm identification belong to neglect.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: How is vision tested in the EMS VAN exam?
options: Ask the patient to follow an object to the left and right
Count fingers held up in all 4 quadrants while the patient looks at your nose
Cover each eye and read a near card
Touch each arm and ask the patient to identify it
questions.explanation: With the patient looking at your nose, hold up varying numbers of fingers in each quadrant (RU, RL, LU, LL), then have them track a finger and report double vision.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: Which two commands does the EMS VAN aphasia test ask the patient to follow?
questions.explanation: VAN aphasia has the patient name two objects, repeat a statement, and follow "close your eyes" and "make a fist"; failing any is positive. "Open your eyes" is a C-STAT LOC command.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient has gaze deviation (cannot look in one direction with both eyes), holds both arms up for 10 seconds, and answers both LOC questions correctly. What is the C-STAT score and result?
questions.explanation: Abnormal gaze alone scores 2 on C-STAT, and a score ≥ 2 is positive with an LVO likely — gaze carries double weight.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient with normal gaze cannot hold an arm up for 10 seconds and misses one LOC question but follows both commands. What is the C-STAT score and result?
questions.explanation: Arm weakness scores 1. LOC is normal if the patient answers both questions OR follows both commands, so LOC scores 0; total 1 is below the ≥ 2 positive threshold.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient has facial droop, an arm that drifts, and a weak grip. What is the LAMS score and result?
questions.explanation: LAMS: droop present 1 + drift 1 + weak grip 1 = 3, below the ≥ 4 LVO threshold. Falls rapidly and no grip each score 2.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient has no facial droop, an arm that falls rapidly, and no grip. What is the LAMS score and result?
questions.explanation: LAMS: droop absent 0 + arm falls rapidly 2 + no grip 2 = 4, meeting the ≥ 4 threshold for LVO even without facial droop.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient has left hemiparesis. While showing the patient the paretic arm, what does the RACE agnosia assessment ask?
questions.explanation: Agnosia is scored for left hemiparesis: ask "Whose arm is this?" while showing the paretic arm, then "Can you lift both arms and clap?" to test recognition of the deficit.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient with left hemiparesis has mild facial palsy, severe arm motor weakness, moderate leg weakness, head/gaze deviation present, and recognizes the arm but not the impairment. What is the RACE score?
questions.explanation: RACE: facial palsy mild 1 + arm severe 2 + leg moderate 1 + gaze deviation present 1 (it has no 2-point level) + agnosia unable to recognize arm or impairment 1 = 6, above the ≥ 5 LVO threshold.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: A patient with right hemiparesis has moderate facial palsy, moderate arm weakness, normal leg strength, no gaze deviation, and performs one of two commands. Does the RACE score suggest a large vessel occlusion?
questions.explanation: RACE: moderate facial palsy 2 + arm moderate 1 + leg 0 + gaze absent 0 + aphasia performs 1 task 1 = 4, below the ≥ 5 LVO threshold.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: For LAPSS screening, how is a screening item answered "unknown" treated?
options: It counts as meeting that criterion
questions.explanation: LAPSS criteria are met when items 4 through 9 are all YES (or unknown), so an unknown seizure history or age does not exclude the patient.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: Which patient finding means LAPSS screening criteria are not met?
questions.explanation: LAPSS requires a history of seizures or epilepsy to be absent (unknown is acceptable); age > 45 and symptoms < 24 hours are criteria that support the screen.

questions.title: Stroke Scales
questions.stem: LAPSS screening criteria are met. What is the next action?
options: Return to the appropriate treatment protocol
Complete the EMS VAN exam before transport
Alert the receiving hospital of a possible stroke
Repeat the full screen after 15 minutes
questions.explanation: A positive LAPSS prompts a pre-arrival stroke alert to the receiving hospital; if not met, return to the appropriate protocol — remembering a stroke is still possible.
